correctness.rationale: The finite matching complex is completely enumerated (f-vector 24,204,744,1116,528,32). A reproducible acyclic Morse matching has 1287 pairs and critical cells (one 0, sixty-five 3, eight 4); all 9936 reversed Hasse incidences are checked. Exact signed Morse gradients produce a diagonal determinant-minus-one eight-by-eight minor, giving integral H3=Z^57 and other reduced groups zero. Signed fixed-face traces for all 48 cube automorphisms give the ten character values; an independent admissible-orbit-cycle sum reproduces them. S4 x C2 character inner products yield all ten multiplicities and the 34/23 antipodal splitting. Ordinary rational quotient homology follows from finite-group averaging after barycentric subdivision. Both scripts executed successfully from package paths and do not assume finite-field ranks imply integral properties.

evidence: Engstrom https://arxiv.org/html/math/0512420v1 proves connectivity and local collapses for claw-free independence complexes; its statements and proofs do not give an explicit cuboctahedral H3 module.

Bate et al. https://arxiv.org/html/2312.13750v3, Theorems 1.1 and 2.1, treat matching complexes of complete hypergraphs and their Sn-modules; C=L(Q3) is a proper 24-edge graph on 12 vertices, not the complete 12-vertex graph.
Freij https://research.aalto.fi/en/publications/equivariant-discrete-morse-theory/ supplies a general equivariant Morse framework but no stated character formula for this specific complex.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The broad matching-complex and equivariant-Morse frameworks allow techniques, not a stronger theorem determining the precise module for an arbitrary subgraph. The 2005 connectivity estimates cannot imply the ten specified character values. Even knowing the previously published sphere count only identifies the character at the identity.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: A general signed fixed-simplex Euler formula reconstructs H3 only after the specific concentration theorem and all 48 finite signed fixed-face counts are established; no checked source supplies these values or an explicit specialization. Thus the proposed full representation is neither a restatement of the 57-sphere wedge nor implied by the different octahedral or configuration-space modules. A general-purpose computation algorithm is distinguished from a previously determined module.

originality.rationale: The complete S4 x C2 character/decomposition of H3 of the ordinary cuboctahedral matching complex is distinct from the previously published nonequivariant wedge-of-57-spheres result. The most plausible same-group and same-graph analogues concern, respectively, the six-vertex octahedral matching complex and the two-particle configuration space of the cuboctahedron, neither of which determines these ten character values. Full primary-text comparisons of the closest sources and explicit implication analysis support best-knowledge originality, with unindexed duplication remaining a risk.
residual_risks: An unindexed or privately circulated computation of the exact cuboctahedral homology character may exist; the database queries do not prove absolute novelty.
The complete publisher full text of Freij was not accessed; the accessible abstract gives a general framework but no same-object indication.
Integral G-module lattice structure and integral quotient homology remain unclassified; these are intentionally outside the claim.

value.rationale: For the canonical highly symmetric cuboctahedral graph, the prior nonequivariant wedge classification leaves its 57-dimensional homology symmetry module unknown. The full ten-class character and ten isotypical multiplicities give a natural complete classification, and the positive one-dimensional full symmetry invariant contrasts with the three-dimensional rotation invariant. Those numbers determine the rational homology of two genuine orbit spaces and are not determined by rank 57 alone. This is an interpretable symmetry invariant of a geometric graph, not an arbitrary combinatorial slice or a previously tabulated Betti number; no larger paper-sized theorem is claimed.
